ego.name: Phillis Wheatley
ego.summary: Phillis Wheatley Peters was a West African-born American poet and the first African-American author to publish a book of poetry. Enslaved as a child in Boston, she received an exceptional classical education, achieved transatlantic recognition with Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773), and later lived in poverty after her emancipation and marriage.

connections.relationship_description: Boston merchant who purchased Wheatley as an enslaved child for his wife, Susanna; the Wheatley household supported her education and the family manumitted her in 1773.
shared_activities: supporting her education and literary work
connections.notes: The relationship was fundamentally coercive: John Wheatley legally enslaved her until her emancipation in 1773.

connections.relationship_description: Wheatley’s enslaver and the woman for whom John Wheatley purchased her; Susanna encouraged Wheatley’s poetry, helped pursue London publication, and was among the Wheatleys who manumitted her.
connections.notes: Susanna's fatal illness prompted Wheatley's return from London before the book's publication.

connections.relationship_description: The Wheatleys' daughter and Wheatley's first tutor in reading and writing; she helped provide the foundation for Wheatley's literary and classical education.
connections.notes: Mary was about 18 when Wheatley entered the household.

connections.relationship_description: Son of the Wheatley household who tutored Wheatley and accompanied her to London in 1773 while her poetry collection was being prepared for publication.
shared_activities: London journey in search of publication
connections.notes: Their London trip was motivated chiefly by the search for a publisher and partly by Wheatley's asthma.

connections.relationship_description: Prominent evangelist whose 1770 death prompted Wheatley's widely circulated elegy, On the Death of the Rev. Mr. George Whitefield, which brought her major public attention.
shared_activities: circulation of the elegy in Boston, Philadelphia, and New Haven
connections.notes: The connection was literary and commemorative rather than a documented personal association.

connections.relationship_description: London bookseller and printer who published Wheatley’s Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral after evidence of her authorship was provided.
shared_activities: printing and publishing Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral
connections.notes: Bell preserved the original Boston attestation for consultation at his Aldgate Street shop.

connections.relationship_description: Boston political leader who was among the prominent men attesting in 1772 that they believed Wheatley had written the poems attributed to her, countering racist doubts about her authorship.
shared_activities: Examination or public attestation of Wheatley's authorship
signing the attestation published with her 1773 collection
connections.notes: The attestation was obtained because London publisher Archibald Bell demanded proof that an enslaved African woman was the poems' author.

connections.relationship_description: Governor of Massachusetts and one of the Boston luminaries who signed the 1772 attestation affirming their belief that Wheatley wrote the poems published under her name.
shared_activities: signing the published attestation for Poems on Various Subjects
connections.notes: His participation reflects the extraordinary racial skepticism Wheatley had to overcome to publish.

connections.relationship_description: Massachusetts lieutenant governor who joined the 1772 group of prominent Bostonians certifying their belief that Wheatley was the author of her poems.
shared_activities: signing the preface attestation to Wheatley's 1773 book
connections.notes: Oliver was listed as lieutenant governor in the published attestation.

connections.relationship_description: English Methodist leader and patron who subsidized Wheatley’s 1773 collection, dedicated to her; they corresponded but did not meet because Hastings was ill.
shared_activities: patronage of Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral
connections.notes: Her financial and social support helped overcome colonial publishers' refusal to publish Wheatley's book.

connections.relationship_description: Enslaved Black artist addressed in Wheatley’s poem To S. M. a young African Painter, on seeing his Works; he may have engraved her book’s frontispiece, but the attribution is uncertain.
shared_activities: possible production of Wheatley's engraved frontispiece
shared Black artistic milieu in Boston
connections.notes: Moorhead is the only Black person explicitly addressed in Wheatley's surviving poetry.

connections.relationship_description: Lord Mayor of London who received Wheatley during her 1773 visit and was among the prominent London figures supporting her growing literary reputation.
connections.notes: Their documented connection appears limited to Wheatley's London visit.

connections.relationship_description: Mohegan Presbyterian minister and advocate for Indigenous and enslaved peoples with whom Wheatley corresponded; she praised his belief that enslaved people should receive their natural-born rights in America.
shared_activities: discussion of natural rights and the condition of enslaved people
connections.notes: Their correspondence gave Wheatley a channel to state antislavery principles directly.

connections.relationship_description: British merchant-philanthropist who exchanged letters with Wheatley and discussed her poetry in correspondence with John Newton.
shared_activities: discussion and circulation of Wheatley's poetry
connections.notes: The available account documents correspondence but does not establish frequent in-person contact.

connections.relationship_description: Continental Army commander to whom Wheatley sent her 1775 poem To His Excellency, George Washington; he praised her poetic talent and invited her to visit his Cambridge headquarters.
shared_activities: Exchange concerning To His Excellency, George Washington
publication of the poem in The Pennsylvania Gazette
connections.notes: Washington's favorable response made him an important elite admirer of Wheatley's work.

connections.relationship_description: Free Black grocer whom Wheatley married in 1778; their household endured severe poverty, Peters’s 1784 debt imprisonment, and the deaths of their three children.
shared_activities: Marriage and shared household in Boston
enduring poverty and Peters's debt imprisonment
connections.notes: Peters was imprisoned for debt in 1784; Wheatley then worked as a scullery maid while caring for their infant son.

connections.relationship_description: Fellow enslaved African-American poet who admired Wheatley and wrote An Address to Miss Phillis Wheatley in 1778, engaging her work through Christian exhortation.
connections.notes: They never met, but Hammon's published address is a significant contemporary Black literary response to Wheatley.

category_summaries.summary: Wheatley's documented family network centers on her marriage to John Peters after emancipation. Their life together was marked by poverty, Peters's debt imprisonment, and the early deaths of their three children.

Wheatley’s formative opportunities arose within the coercive Wheatley household, where she was enslaved but received rare instruction from Mary and Nathaniel Wheatley and support from John and Susanna. Her route to publication also required elite validation, notably the 1772 attestation signed by Hancock, Hutchinson, Oliver, and others.

Wheatley's literary network was transatlantic: London patrons and publisher Archibald Bell enabled her landmark 1773 collection, while prominent readers and correspondents validated, circulated, and responded to her work. Her links to Scipio Moorhead and Jupiter Hammon are especially significant as connections with fellow Black artists and writers.
